## Paper

## Abstract

The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to chemical discovery is critically hindered by the
inaccessibility of data locked within unstructured scientific literature. Existing data acquisition methods are often
manual, limited in scope, or require extensive custom software development, impeding progress in leveraging
AI for chemical discovery. Here, we introduce ReactionSeek, a framework that synergistically combines large
language models (LLMs) with established cheminformatics tools to automate multi-modal data mining from
organic synthesis literature. Through sophisticated prompt engineering with minimal custom code, ReactionSeek
extracts and standardizes complex textual, graphical, and semantic chemical information. We validate this
framework on the century-spanning Organic Syntheses collection, achieving over 95% precision and recall for
key reaction parameters. This enables three applications: the generation of a large, AI-ready dataset; an
interactive Synthetic Chatbot (SynChat) for natural language querying of chemical data; and an autonomous
analysis that revealed decades-long trends in catalysis. ReactionSeek thus provides a general solution to the data
curation bottleneck, representing a step forward in for AI-driven archive mining and knowledge discovery across
the chemical sciences.

---

## Introduction

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the molecular sciences is poised to fundamentally reshape
discovery, accelerating innovation from medicine to materials.1 This potential is particularly crucial in organic
synthesis, the foundational discipline of molecular construction.2 While AI-driven strategies have demonstrated
notable capabilities in retrosynthetic planning, mechanistic studies, and the discovery of novel reactions,3 their
application to the frontiers of chemical research is hampered by data accessibility. The vast majority of our
chemical knowledge, painstakingly accumulated over a century, remains locked within unstructured literature.
This forces a reliance on curated, often proprietary datasets, meaning that current AI models are trained on
sanitized information that fails to capture the complexity and diversity of real-world chemistry.4 Therefore,
creating automated and scalable methods to convert this immense scientific legacy into actionable, machine-
readable knowledge is the rate-limiting step toward unlocking genuine, AI-driven discovery in chemistry.5

Current approaches to data acquisition each present significant limitations. Commercial databases, while
extensive, are often constrained by data inconsistencies, incomplete coverage of specialized reaction types, and
restrictive licensing terms. High-throughput experimentation (HTE), on the other hand, generates precise
datasets that typically lack chemical diversity and are prohibitively expensive for many research groups.6,7 As a
result, manual curation from the scientific literature remains a common practice for building domain-specific
datasets. This approach is not only labor-intensive and time-consuming but also requires specific chemical
expertise and is prone to human error, potentially compromising dataset quality and scalability. Therefore, a
pressing need exists for an automated, reliable, and scalable methodology to address this data curation
bottleneck.8

Early efforts to automate chemical data extraction have explored various natural language processing (NLP)
techniques.9 Rule-based and traditional machine learning models struggled with the nuanced language of
chemical texts, particularly the complexity of molecular nomenclature, reaction schemes, and the implicit
knowledge embedded in experimental descriptions.10 Recently, large language models (LLMs) have
demonstrated significant promise due to their advanced text comprehension abilities.11-18 However, compared to
data mining efforts in related domains such as materials and biological sciences, mining organic synthesis
presents substantial challenges(Fig. 1a). This task requires interpreting not only diverse molecular structures and
identifiers but also the complex, context-dependent relationships among them. This goes beyond generic text
comprehension; it necessitates a framework that can effectively leverage the LLM's latent knowledge of
chemistry and reasoning abilities. While recent studies have utilized LLMs through methods such as fine-
tuning,11,13,15,19,20 prompt engineering,12,16-18,21,22 and other approaches,23-28 these pioneering methods often face
limitations. Key issues include a lack of adaptability across different literature styles, overly complex
implementations, and the considerable computational cost of model fine-tuning. Additionally, previous LLM-
based reaction mining approaches still face several challenges, including: the dispersion of compound
information across sub-headings, the conversion of chemical names to SMILES notation, complex compound
references, and the identification of compounds in reference images.29 Consequently, there remains a persistent
need for a more universal and resource-efficient methodology tailored to the intricacies of organic synthesis data
mining.

To tackle these challenges, we introduce ReactionSeek. This framework automates the multi-modal
extraction of chemical data from scientific literature (Fig. 1b). It employs a hybrid architecture that combines
the contextual understanding of LLMs with the chemical precision of established cheminformatics tools.
ReactionSeek utilizes a domain-specific prompt engineering strategy, enabling robust and accurate data mining
without the need for resource-intensive model fine-tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of
this approach by systematically mining the entire century-spanning Organic Syntheses collection30, achieving
over 95% precision and recall for key reaction parameters. The resulting AI-ready dataset enabled two
downstream applications: the development of SynChat, an interactive chatbot for querying reaction data via
natural language, and an autonomous, LLM-driven analysis that successfully identified decades-long historical
trends in catalysis. Thus, ReactionSeek provides a solid and transferable solution to the data curation bottleneck,
paving the way for large-scale, AI-driven knowledge discovery across the chemical sciences.

---

## Results

The ReactionSeek Data Mining Framework

ReactionSeek is designed to process chemical literature to extract and organize reaction information,
transforming raw textual and graphical data into a curated, machine-readable dataset (Fig. 1b). The workflow
comprises three core stages: (1) Image mining for interpreting reaction schemes and structures within figures;
(2) Text mining for extracting detailed experimental information from procedural text using prompt-engineered
LLMs; and (3) Data standardization for ensuring the accuracy and consistency of the extracted chemical entities
and reaction parameters.

Organic Chemistry Image Mining: The accurate interpretation of chemical structures and reaction schemes
depicted in images is a foundational challenge in automated chemical data mining. While existing Optical
Character Structure Recognition (OCSR) tools can convert molecular structures into machine-readable formats
(e.g., SMILES),24,25,31-33 associating these structures with their correct roles (e.g., reactant, product) and textual
identifiers within complex figures remains a daunting challenge. ReactionSeek addresses this by employing a
multi-modal LLM (GLM-4V) to analyze reaction scheme images (Fig. 2a). The LLM is prompted to identify
compound labels within the image and map them to the corresponding molecular structure images, which are
subsequently converted to SMILES by OCSR tools (e.g., InDraw34).

To evaluate this image mining module, we tested it on 42 diverse reaction scheme images sourced from the
supplementary information (SI) of published literature. The multi-modal LLM (GLM-4V) achieved 91.5%
accuracy in correctly identifying and associating the molecular labels and their roles of reactants or products.
The InDraw OCSR tool was used to convert the molecular images to SMILES with 70.1% accuracy (see more
details in Supplementary Note 1.1).34 While the overall performance is promising, the accuracy of structure
recognition is influenced by the capabilities of the currently integrated OCSR tool, suggesting potential for
improvement with more accurate OCSR solutions.

Organic Chemistry Text Mining: Extracting detailed experimental procedures and reaction parameters from
unstructured text is central to ReactionSeek. To achieve this with high fidelity and minimal human intervention,
we developed a sophisticated prompt engineering pipeline for LLMs (Fig. 2b). This pipeline adapts general-
purpose LLMs to the specific nuances of organic chemistry literature, guiding them to extract predefined
chemical information and structure into a tabulated format suitable for review and downstream processing. With
this pipeline, the LLM can effectively identify compound entities within text segments and establish their
complex co-reference relationships. By processing sub-headings and text segments separately, our pipeline
successfully achieves the association between compound references in synthetic text segments and the
corresponding compounds mentioned in sub-headings.

Our prompt architecture, inspired by previous work on MOF data extraction,17 comprises four key
components designed to optimize LLM performance in this domain-specific task (see more details in
Supplementary Note 4.1): (1) Task description: This component clearly defines the overall objective of the
data mining task and provides fundamental guidelines to the LLM, including instructions to mitigate common
issues like output hallucination. (2) Task requirements: Here, we specify the information to be extracted and the
output format (e.g., a table with specific columns). This section is strategically placed to reinforce the LLM's
adherence to output specifications, countering potential memory decay with long inputs. (3) Processing
suggestions: This provides the LLM with expert-derived heuristics in natural language. These suggestions are
based on a pre-examination of sample texts by domain experts, who summarize common textual patterns and
incorporate essential chemical knowledge to aid the LLM in interpreting chemical narratives. (4) Processing
cases: Few-shot examples, consisting of real input texts and their corresponding desired structured outputs, are
provided. This allows the LLM to learn the specific input-output patterns and formatting requirements through
in-context learning. This structured prompting approach is designed to ensure the LLM maintains a balance of
task memory, semantic comprehension of the chemical context, and accurate execution of the extraction task.

To validate our data mining pipeline, we benchmarked its performance on the authoritative ChEMU35-38).
This selection ensures a rigorous comparative analysis, as state-of-the-art models from the ChEMU-2022
competition have explicitly established a high-performance baseline (F1 = 0.968) on this specific dataset. Our
pipeline demonstrated a remarkable advantage in the few-shot learning scenario. With only seven annotated
examples, it achieved an F1 score of 0.983 in extracting critical reaction components, including reactants,
products, solvents, temperature, time, and yield, representing a further improvement over the previous model
(see more details in Supplementary Note 3.3 Table S1).

The text mining efficacy of GLM-4 was also evaluated using a benchmark dataset of 50 reactions obtained
from the Supporting Information (SI) of six diverse articles on organic synthesis (see more details in SI
References). The extraction results were classified as true positives (TPS; correctly identified entities or values),
false negatives (FN; omissions), and false positives (FP; incorrect or fabricated information). In synthetic
chemistry applications, FPs are typically considered more detrimental than FNs. Our prompting strategy
effectively guided the model to extract a variety of experimental data, including compound identifiers, quantities,
yields, solvents, reaction conditions, and enantiomeric excess (e.e.) values, achieving high precision, recall, and
F1 scores for nearly all categories(see more details in Supplementary Note 4.1 Table 2) The only discrepancy
was the misidentification of an uncommon solvent mixture or additive (e.g., 18-crown-6), indicating that the
model's performance critically relies on its pre-existing chemical knowledge. This limitation can be easily
addressed by enhancing the prompt with information about such uncommon entities.

The text mining pipeline was subsequently expanded to extract complex spectroscopic data (NMR, MS,
HPLC) by leveraging tailored prompts with GPT-4. We targeted characterization data for 236 molecules from
the SI of the same benchmark literature used previously and developed prompts for data mining, including 1H
NMR, MS, HPLC, and IR (see more details in SI 3.1-3.2). The system demonstrated high efficacy, with
extraction accuracies exceeding 95% for most spectroscopic types (Fig. 3a). Notably, despite the inherent
complexity of 1H NMR data, which requires parsing chemical shifts, splitting patterns, and coupling constants,
the accuracy of its extraction remained remarkably high. This success suggests that the structured prompts
enabled the LLM to effectively extract the in-context chemical knowledge inherent in spectroscopic reports (Fig.
3c). Error analysis highlighted challenges in classifying coupling constants (J-values) and resolving ambiguities
due to inconsistent compound labels. Subsequent analysis indicated that more advanced LLM architectures
exhibit greater robustness against such inconsistencies.

Standardization of Extracted Chemical Information: The conversion of diverse compound nomenclature
(including IUPAC names, common names, misspelled variants, and chemical formulas) into machine-readable
SMILES representations remains a significant challenge in organic reaction mining29. A critical component of
ReactionSeek is its data standardization module, which is designed to convert raw extracted text into an accurate,
consistent, and AI-ready format (Fig. 2c). The module emphasizes two primary curation tasks: name-to-SMILES
transformation and unit standardization.

General-purpose LLMs are often unreliable for direct name-to-SMILES transformation, a limitation rooted
in their generative instability and lack of domain-specific knowledge training. As reported in previous work39 ,
this deficiency results in a high frequency of critical errors, including unparsable strings, the addition or omission
of atoms, incorrect functional group placement, and erroneous backbone structures. Given these significant
reliability issues, the direct application of general-purpose LLMs for this conversion task is challenging.
ReactionSeek overcomes this by implementing a hybrid workflow: (1) First, unique compound names are
compiled from the mining results. (2) Second, these names are processed using established cheminformatics
resources, including database lookups (e.g., PubChem40) and name-to-structure converters (e.g., OPSIN41), to
generate canonical SMILES. (3) Finally, the LLM, enhanced with vector and fuzzy search capabilities,
intelligently maps the mined nomenclature, which is often non-standardized, to the canonical SMILES curated
by these specialized tools. This iterative process of data validation, parsing, and LLM-assisted alignment ensures
the generation of high-fidelity structural representations (Fig. 2c).

Simultaneously, the module leverages the LLM in unit standardization (Fig. 2c). Through carefully
designed prompts, it standardizes units for all reaction parameters (e.g., time, temperature) to ensure dataset-
wide consistency. The final output is a structured CSV file that summarizes each reaction using standardized
identifiers and parameters. This curated dataset is not only directly suitable for building predictive models but
also serves as the knowledge base for interactive tools such as the SynChat application.

Large-Scale Reaction Mining: A Case Study of the Organic Syntheses Collection30
To demonstrate the scalability and practical utility of ReactionSeek, we applied it to the systematic mining
of the Organic Syntheses collection30, a historically significant and high-quality repository of verified synthetic
procedures published since 1921. This collection, comprising 102 volumes as of 2025, represents a valuable
resource for studying the evolution of synthetic methodology. For this study, we processed 3,103 articles from
the first 100 volumes, establishing a comprehensive raw dataset for subsequent analysis and chatbot development
(see more details in Supplementary Figure 4). A benchmark subset of 50 articles from this collection was also
curated manually for detailed performance evaluation.

Efficiency of Automated Mining: A key advantage of ReactionSeek is its potential to significantly reduce
the time and effort associated with manual data extraction. On the 50-article benchmark set, using GLM-442, the
framework required an average of 21.32 seconds per article for data mining and output formatting. This
represents a substantial improvement over manual data mining, which typically requires 5-10 minutes or longer
per article, underscoring the efficiency gains enabled by our LLM-based approach.

Accuracy Assessment on Organic Syntheses30 Benchmark: We evaluated the accuracy of ReactionSeek
(with GLM-4) on the 50-article benchmark dataset, employing evaluation criteria tailored to the practical needs
of subsequent applications. (1) Reactants and Products: Correct and complete extraction and classification of all
compound entities involved as reactants or products were considered critical. (2) Reaction Yield: Precise
extraction of yield values. (3) Reaction Scale (Amounts): The focus was on accurately extracting amounts for
key reactants and products, with relaxed stringency for ancillary reagents, such as solvents or excess reagents,
where order-of-magnitude and proportional relationships are often sufficient. (4) Time and Temperature: Given
the potential variability in experimental records for these parameters, the model was assessed on its ability to
extract the critical time and temperature values it deemed necessary, rather than achieving absolute accuracy for
every recorded value.

As shown in Fig. 4a, GLM-4 demonstrated strong performance in compound identification, particularly for
products, with very few FPs in reactant extraction, meeting a key accuracy demand. However, some omissions
(FNs) occurred during reactant extraction, likely due to inconsistent textual positioning of reactants. The
occurrence of FPs in solvent identification suggested the LLM might rely on its a priori knowledge of common
solvents, potentially misclassifying uncommon solvents or reactants.

In numerical data extraction, the model showed high accuracy for reaction yields and product quantities,
with no instances of hallucinated yield values on the test set. A notable error pattern emerged in reactant quantity
extraction when a compound was added in multiple portions; the model often struggled to accurately aggregate
these amounts. This may reflect limitations in the LLM's complex numerical reasoning within linguistic contexts
or the absence of specific prompt engineering for such scenarios. Time and temperature extraction, although
facing similar complexities, benefited from being listed as separate extraction targets, resulting in comparatively
better performance.

Out of the 50 benchmark articles, 48 yielded outputs conforming to the required format after reprocessing
of any initially unparseable results. The two articles that failed to produce correctly formatted outputs were
significantly longer (9824 and 5502 characters, which may almost exceed the context window of the LLM) and
contained more reactions (5 reactions each) than average. In these cases, GLM-4 successfully extracted the
information but failed in formatting, suggesting that very long input texts following an already lengthy prompt
can lead to the model partially forgetting initial formatting instructions.43 Text segmentation is a potential
strategy to mitigate this issue.

Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Text Mining : The performance of LLM-based data mining is
significantly influenced by the choice of the underlying model, particularly its parameter size and architecture.
To guide model selection for ReactionSeek, we evaluated a diverse range of LLMs on the Organic Syntheses30
benchmark dataset. The models tested included GLM-4, GPT-3.544, GPT-445, Llama46, Mixtral47, Baichuan48,
Qwen49, and DeepSeek50.

Larger models generally exhibited significantly higher performance in extracting chemical information (Fig.
4a, 4d). This suggests that increased parameter size critically impacts an LLM's ability to understand complex
chemical contents. Larger models were better at understanding task objectives and correctly identifying relevant
chemical entities. Furthermore, the incidence of unparseable or incorrectly formatted responses decreased with
increasing model size (Fig. 4b). This improvement is likely due to the enhanced capacity of larger models to
handle long token inputs while retaining memory of key prompt instructions, and their superior ability to
comprehend complex chemical relationships and knowledge inherent in the context.

Interestingly, while larger models excelled in precision, medium-sized models often achieved comparable
recall rates (Fig. 4c). This indicates that once a model possesses a sufficient parameter scale to grasp the
fundamental chemical tasks outlined in the prompts, further size increases may offer diminishing profit for
simple identification tasks. Persistent error types, such as the aggregation of reactant quantities from multiple
additions, were not fully resolved solely by increasing model parameter size, highlighting the need for targeted
prompt refinements or algorithmic solutions for such specific challenges (Fig. 4b-d).

Analysis of successful extractions by small and medium-sized models revealed they typically performed
well in articles describing simpler reactions (e.g., fewer compounds, straightforward single-step procedures) and
those with shorter text lengths. This suggests that text segment length is a key factor influencing an LLM's ability
to generate valid, well-formatted outputs, as shorter texts reduce the cognitive and memory burden on the model.
For less complex extraction tasks or when using smaller models, strategies such as text segmentation or
employing models specifically adapted for long contexts can improve performance.

Based on the aforementioned evaluations, we ultimately employed GPT-3.5-16k to conduct data mining on
Organic Syntheses30 volumes 1–100, spanning from 1921 to 2021. After complete pipeline processing and
deduplication, we obtained 5,443 unique compounds, 3,961 unique reactions, of which 3,580 contained yield
information.

To demonstrate our pipeline's generalizability to newly published literature, we tested it on all newly
published articles (29 articles) from the 2025 volume of Organic Syntheses30 (Fig. 4e and Table 1). Our pipeline
correctly extracting most of reaction information from each article. During the standardization phase, with the
exception of molecular sieves that cannot be directly represented as SMILES, all other compounds were
successfully converted into their correct corresponding SMILES representations. These results confirm our
pipeline’s robustness, showing its ability to generalize effectively from benchmark datasets to newly published
chemical literature.

While modest in size compared to larger reaction databases like USSPTO, the value of our minded dataset
lies not in its breadth, but in its curated depth. It is composed of the most representative and classical organic
reactions across one century, with the exclusive inclusion of gram-scale procedures guaranteeing experimental
robustness and reproducibility. Consequently, we propose that this collection can serve as a standardized
reference for synthetic chemists and as a high-fidelity benchmark for the development and validation of machine
learning models.

LLM-Driven Discovery of Chemical Trends from Mined Data
To demonstrate the potential for data-driven discovery, we utilized ReactionSeek to create a large-scale,
structured dataset from the Organic Syntheses30 collection. This AI-ready dataset then served as the input for
autonomous analysis via Gemini 2.5 Pro.51 By designing specific prompts, we tasked the LLM with uncovering
historical trends within this century-spanning compendium, including the emergence and diversification of
asymmetric catalysis and the changing landscape of metal utilization in synthesis (Fig. 5).

In its analysis of asymmetric catalysis (Fig. 5b), the LLM identified a significant increase in such reactions
after 1980. It highlighted the pivotal role of transition-metal catalysts, alongside the emergence of organic small-
molecule catalysts and enzymatic/biocatalytic systems. The LLM noted the prevalent use of specific metals like
Boron, Copper, Titanium, Ruthenium, and Palladium, correlating their use with advancements in well-known
methodologies such as CBS reductions, metal-coupling protocols, asymmetric epoxidation (e.g., with Titanium
Tartrate or Ti-BINOL systems), asymmetric hydrogenation, cross-coupling reactions, and allylic alkylation.
Furthermore, the LLM identified substrate preferences, observing that aldehydes and ketones, as well as halides,
were the most dominant, with esters and alkenes also featuring prominently (see Supplementary Note 2.4 for
more details).

Regarding metal usage trends (Fig. 5b, 5d), the LLM's analysis revealed an interesting prevalence of tin in
specific periods, correctly attributing this to the widespread adoption of tributyltin hydride (Bu3SnH) as a mild
radical initiator, reducing agent, and key component in Stille couplings. More broadly, the LLM categorized the
evolution of metal usage in Organic Syntheses30 into three distinct epochs: (1) The Main-Group Metal Era (1921–
1960): Dominated by Grignard reagents and salt-forming reactions, with less emphasis on metal toxicity. (2) The
Incipient Transition (1961–1990): Characterized by the rise of lithium/copper reagents, the early development
of palladium catalysis, and a decline in mercury utilization. (3) The Golden Age of Transition-Metal Catalysis
(1991–2023): Marked by concentrated growth in Palladium-, Ruthenium-, and Rhodium-mediated
transformations.

These LLM-identified trends accurately reflect established paradigm shifts in organic synthesis from
stoichiometric to catalytic approaches, from harsh to milder conditions, and from highly toxic reagents towards
greener methodologies. This demonstrates that an LLM, when provided with a structured dataset curated by
ReactionSeek, can autonomously develop analytical insights and perform trend analyses consistent with expert
chemical knowledge, highlighting the potential for AI-assisted discovery from systematically mined literature.

The Synthesis Chatbot: Interactive Access to Mined Knowledge
To enhance the accessibility and utility of the extensive dataset curated from Organic Syntheses30, we
developed SynChat, an interactive tool powered by LLM agents. SynChat allows researchers to query the
historical reaction data and associated metadata using natural language, providing a more intuitive and efficient
means of accessing specific data compared to traditional search methodology.

The development of the chatbot involved structuring the mined data for effective retrieval by the LLM. Key
information from each reaction entry (e.g., title, DOI, reactants, products, SMILES, yield) was compiled and
vectorized to a customized vector database52.This allows the LLM, when presented with a user query, to perform
similarity searches across the Vector Database and retrieve the most relevant supporting texts from the original
Organic Syntheses30 (Fig. 6). The LLM agent then synthesizes an answer based on this retrieved information,
previous record and reasoning, with prompts designed to ensure strict adherence to the source material, thereby
minimizing the likelihood of generating hallucinated or inaccurate responses.

SynChat offers several advantages for chemical researchers: (1) Natural Language Queries with Molecular
Structures: It handles complex queries posed in natural language that incorporate molecular structures or reaction
information, increasing the flexibility of data access for users without specialized database query language skills.
(2) Enhanced Reliability and Traceability: By citing specific data sources from the Organic Syntheses30
collection, the chatbot allows users to consult the original literature for verification and further context easily.
(3) Iterative Information Retrieval: The interactive nature of the LLM enables users to refine their queries or ask
follow-up questions in multi-turn dialogues, facilitating a more thorough exploration of the available information.
This interactive tool exemplifies how LLMs can transform structured and unstructured data into dynamic
knowledge resources, bringing AI-powered assistance directly into the research and learning workflows of
organic chemists.

---

## Methods

Prompt Design for Image Mining
Image mining was conducted using the GLM-4V multi-modal large language model. To improve the logical
accuracy of the model in determining compound roles, we designed specific instructions requiring the LLM to
explicitly analyze the visual orientation of reaction arrows (e.g., distinguishing between reactants and products
based on arrow direction). Adopting the structured prompt framework utilized in our text mining workflow, the
image mining prompts were specifically tailored to extract the numerical labels associated with reactants,
products, and reagents from the reaction schemes. Following role identification, chemical structure recognition
was performed using InDraw,34 which automatically segmented and identified each compound structure before
converting them into canonical SMILES strings for storage. Full details regarding the prompt engineering
strategies and templates are provided in Supplementary Note 1.1.

Prompt Design for Text Mining
To extract detailed experimental procedures and reaction parameters from unstructured organic chemistry
literature with high fidelity, we developed a structured prompt engineering pipeline tailored for Large Language
Models (LLMs). This pipeline was designed to guide the LLM in identifying compound entities, resolving co-
reference relationships, and structuring extracted data into a standardized tabular format. The prompt architecture,
inspired by methodologies for metal-organic framework (MOF) data extraction17, consists of four strategic
components optimized for chemical text analysis:

1. Task Description: This module defines the global objective of the data mining task. It includes explicit
constraints and negative constraints to mitigate common LLM issues, such as hallucination, ensuring
the model focuses strictly on the provided text.
2. Task Requirements: To ensure output consistency, this module specifies the exact information fields to
be extracted and enforces a strict tabular output format. This instruction block is strategically positioned
within the prompt to reinforce the LLM’s adherence to formatting specifications, thereby counteracting
potential context forgetting (memory decay) associated with long input sequences.
3. Processing Suggestions: We incorporated expert-derived heuristics in natural language to aid the LLM.
These suggestions were developed through a pre-examination of representative literature by domain
experts, summarizing common textual patterns and embedding essential chemical knowledge to
facilitate the correct interpretation of complex chemical narratives.
4. Processing Cases (Few-Shot Learning): To facilitate in-context learning, we included a set of few-shot
examples consisting of raw input texts paired with their corresponding, manually verified structured
outputs. This module allows the LLM to learn specific input-output mappings and formatting
requirements by example.

To resolve complex co-reference relationships, the pipeline processes sub-headings and main text segments as
distinct but related inputs, enabling the model to associate compound references within the synthetic procedures
with their corresponding specific compounds defined in the sub-headings. Full details of the prompt templates
and specific examples are provided in Supplementary Note 1.2.

Data Standardization Design
The standardization process was carried out in three consecutive steps. In step (1), the chemical compound
dataset was created using compound names and their respective CAS numbers extracted from the Organic
Syntheses30 collection. Next, in step (2), compound identifiers were primarily obtained through CAS numbers,
followed by additional identification using PubChem40 nomenclature and OPSIN41 systematic name parsing for
unprocessed entries. In step (3), molecular name vectorization was conducted to produce a comprehensive
dataset, which allowed for precise matching of mined molecular names. For unit standardization, temporal values
were consistently converted into minutes, with particular attention given to unconventional temporal expressions,
such as "overnight". Similarly, material quantities were standardized by converting all measurements into
uniform units of grams and moles. Full details regarding the prompt engineering strategies and templates are
provided in Supplementary Note 1.1.

Design of SynChat
The reaction database is architected into two distinct components to optimize retrieval efficiency and
information density: a vectorized query database for semantic search and a supplementary metadata repository
for detailed experimental context.

(1) Vectorization and Indexing: Key retrieval fields—including product SMILES, ReactionSMILES,
chemical nomenclature, reaction types, and article titles—were vectorized using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model,
a Sentence-BERT (SBERT) framework. This model transforms input text into 384-dimensional dense vector
embeddings without dimensionality reduction. These embeddings were indexed and managed using
ChromaDB53, an open-source vector database, to facilitate high-speed semantic similarity search. The specific
distribution of these embedding vectors is visualized in Supplementary Note 5.

(2) Data Retrieval and Generation: Detailed experimental parameters, including full synthetic procedures,
yields, reagent quantities, reaction conditions, and citation metadata, are stored in the supplementary database in
a JSON file. Upon receiving a user query, the system executes a retrieval process that identifies relevant entries
based on vector similarity (semantic match) and exact character matching within the ChromaDB index. The
system then retrieves the corresponding comprehensive procedural details from the supplementary database.
Finally, the retrieved context—combining the concise query features and the full textual descriptions—is
concatenated and fed into the Large Language Model (LLM). This Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
approach enables the LLM to generate tailored, evidence-based responses to user inquiries regarding specific
reaction conditions and procedures.

## Paper

## Abstract

The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to chemical discovery is critically hindered by the
inaccessibility of data locked within unstructured scientific literature. Existing data acquisition methods are often
manual, limited in scope, or require extensive custom software development, impeding progress in leveraging
AI for chemical discovery. Here, we introduce ReactionSeek, a framework that synergistically combines large
language models (LLMs) with established cheminformatics tools to automate multi-modal data mining from
organic synthesis literature. Through sophisticated prompt engineering with minimal custom code, ReactionSeek
extracts and standardizes complex textual, graphical, and semantic chemical information. We validate this
framework on the century-spanning Organic Syntheses collection, achieving over 95% precision and recall for
key reaction parameters. This enables three applications: the generation of a large, AI-ready dataset; an
interactive Synthetic Chatbot (SynChat) for natural language querying of chemical data; and an autonomous
analysis that revealed decades-long trends in catalysis. ReactionSeek thus provides a general solution to the data
curation bottleneck, representing a step forward in for AI-driven archive mining and knowledge discovery across
the chemical sciences.

---

## Introduction

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the molecular sciences is poised to fundamentally reshape
discovery, accelerating innovation from medicine to materials.1 This potential is particularly crucial in organic
synthesis, the foundational discipline of molecular construction.2 While AI-driven strategies have demonstrated
notable capabilities in retrosynthetic planning, mechanistic studies, and the discovery of novel reactions,3 their
application to the frontiers of chemical research is hampered by data accessibility. The vast majority of our
chemical knowledge, painstakingly accumulated over a century, remains locked within unstructured literature.
This forces a reliance on curated, often proprietary datasets, meaning that current AI models are trained on
sanitized information that fails to capture the complexity and diversity of real-world chemistry.4 Therefore,
creating automated and scalable methods to convert this immense scientific legacy into actionable, machine-
readable knowledge is the rate-limiting step toward unlocking genuine, AI-driven discovery in chemistry.5

Current approaches to data acquisition each present significant limitations. Commercial databases, while
extensive, are often constrained by data inconsistencies, incomplete coverage of specialized reaction types, and
restrictive licensing terms. High-throughput experimentation (HTE), on the other hand, generates precise
datasets that typically lack chemical diversity and are prohibitively expensive for many research groups.6,7 As a
result, manual curation from the scientific literature remains a common practice for building domain-specific
datasets. This approach is not only labor-intensive and time-consuming but also requires specific chemical
expertise and is prone to human error, potentially compromising dataset quality and scalability. Therefore, a
pressing need exists for an automated, reliable, and scalable methodology to address this data curation
bottleneck.8

Early efforts to automate chemical data extraction have explored various natural language processing (NLP)
techniques.9 Rule-based and traditional machine learning models struggled with the nuanced language of
chemical texts, particularly the complexity of molecular nomenclature, reaction schemes, and the implicit
knowledge embedded in experimental descriptions.10 Recently, large language models (LLMs) have
demonstrated significant promise due to their advanced text comprehension abilities.11-18 However, compared to
data mining efforts in related domains such as materials and biological sciences, mining organic synthesis
presents substantial challenges(Fig. 1a). This task requires interpreting not only diverse molecular structures and
identifiers but also the complex, context-dependent relationships among them. This goes beyond generic text
comprehension; it necessitates a framework that can effectively leverage the LLM's latent knowledge of
chemistry and reasoning abilities. While recent studies have utilized LLMs through methods such as fine-
tuning,11,13,15,19,20 prompt engineering,12,16-18,21,22 and other approaches,23-28 these pioneering methods often face
limitations. Key issues include a lack of adaptability across different literature styles, overly complex
implementations, and the considerable computational cost of model fine-tuning. Additionally, previous LLM-
based reaction mining approaches still face several challenges, including: the dispersion of compound
information across sub-headings, the conversion of chemical names to SMILES notation, complex compound
references, and the identification of compounds in reference images.29 Consequently, there remains a persistent
need for a more universal and resource-efficient methodology tailored to the intricacies of organic synthesis data
mining.

To tackle these challenges, we introduce ReactionSeek. This framework automates the multi-modal
extraction of chemical data from scientific literature (Fig. 1b). It employs a hybrid architecture that combines
the contextual understanding of LLMs with the chemical precision of established cheminformatics tools.
ReactionSeek utilizes a domain-specific prompt engineering strategy, enabling robust and accurate data mining
without the need for resource-intensive model fine-tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of
this approach by systematically mining the entire century-spanning Organic Syntheses collection30, achieving
over 95% precision and recall for key reaction parameters. The resulting AI-ready dataset enabled two
downstream applications: the development of SynChat, an interactive chatbot for querying reaction data via
natural language, and an autonomous, LLM-driven analysis that successfully identified decades-long historical
trends in catalysis. Thus, ReactionSeek provides a solid and transferable solution to the data curation bottleneck,
paving the way for large-scale, AI-driven knowledge discovery across the chemical sciences.

---

## Results

The ReactionSeek Data Mining Framework

ReactionSeek is designed to process chemical literature to extract and organize reaction information,
transforming raw textual and graphical data into a curated, machine-readable dataset (Fig. 1b). The workflow
comprises three core stages: (1) Image mining for interpreting reaction schemes and structures within figures;
(2) Text mining for extracting detailed experimental information from procedural text using prompt-engineered
LLMs; and (3) Data standardization for ensuring the accuracy and consistency of the extracted chemical entities
and reaction parameters.

Organic Chemistry Image Mining: The accurate interpretation of chemical structures and reaction schemes
depicted in images is a foundational challenge in automated chemical data mining. While existing Optical
Character Structure Recognition (OCSR) tools can convert molecular structures into machine-readable formats
(e.g., SMILES),24,25,31-33 associating these structures with their correct roles (e.g., reactant, product) and textual
identifiers within complex figures remains a daunting challenge. ReactionSeek addresses this by employing a
multi-modal LLM (GLM-4V) to analyze reaction scheme images (Fig. 2a). The LLM is prompted to identify
compound labels within the image and map them to the corresponding molecular structure images, which are
subsequently converted to SMILES by OCSR tools (e.g., InDraw34).

To evaluate this image mining module, we tested it on 42 diverse reaction scheme images sourced from the
supplementary information (SI) of published literature. The multi-modal LLM (GLM-4V) achieved 91.5%
accuracy in correctly identifying and associating the molecular labels and their roles of reactants or products.
The InDraw OCSR tool was used to convert the molecular images to SMILES with 70.1% accuracy (see more
details in Supplementary Note 1.1).34 While the overall performance is promising, the accuracy of structure
recognition is influenced by the capabilities of the currently integrated OCSR tool, suggesting potential for
improvement with more accurate OCSR solutions.

Organic Chemistry Text Mining: Extracting detailed experimental procedures and reaction parameters from
unstructured text is central to ReactionSeek. To achieve this with high fidelity and minimal human intervention,
we developed a sophisticated prompt engineering pipeline for LLMs (Fig. 2b). This pipeline adapts general-
purpose LLMs to the specific nuances of organic chemistry literature, guiding them to extract predefined
chemical information and structure into a tabulated format suitable for review and downstream processing. With
this pipeline, the LLM can effectively identify compound entities within text segments and establish their
complex co-reference relationships. By processing sub-headings and text segments separately, our pipeline
successfully achieves the association between compound references in synthetic text segments and the
corresponding compounds mentioned in sub-headings.

Our prompt architecture, inspired by previous work on MOF data extraction,17 comprises four key
components designed to optimize LLM performance in this domain-specific task (see more details in
Supplementary Note 4.1): (1) Task description: This component clearly defines the overall objective of the
data mining task and provides fundamental guidelines to the LLM, including instructions to mitigate common
issues like output hallucination. (2) Task requirements: Here, we specify the information to be extracted and the
output format (e.g., a table with specific columns). This section is strategically placed to reinforce the LLM's
adherence to output specifications, countering potential memory decay with long inputs. (3) Processing
suggestions: This provides the LLM with expert-derived heuristics in natural language. These suggestions are
based on a pre-examination of sample texts by domain experts, who summarize common textual patterns and
incorporate essential chemical knowledge to aid the LLM in interpreting chemical narratives. (4) Processing
cases: Few-shot examples, consisting of real input texts and their corresponding desired structured outputs, are
provided. This allows the LLM to learn the specific input-output patterns and formatting requirements through
in-context learning. This structured prompting approach is designed to ensure the LLM maintains a balance of
task memory, semantic comprehension of the chemical context, and accurate execution of the extraction task.

To validate our data mining pipeline, we benchmarked its performance on the authoritative ChEMU35-38).
This selection ensures a rigorous comparative analysis, as state-of-the-art models from the ChEMU-2022
competition have explicitly established a high-performance baseline (F1 = 0.968) on this specific dataset. Our
pipeline demonstrated a remarkable advantage in the few-shot learning scenario. With only seven annotated
examples, it achieved an F1 score of 0.983 in extracting critical reaction components, including reactants,
products, solvents, temperature, time, and yield, representing a further improvement over the previous model
(see more details in Supplementary Note 3.3 Table S1).

The text mining efficacy of GLM-4 was also evaluated using a benchmark dataset of 50 reactions obtained
from the Supporting Information (SI) of six diverse articles on organic synthesis (see more details in SI
References). The extraction results were classified as true positives (TPS; correctly identified entities or values),
false negatives (FN; omissions), and false positives (FP; incorrect or fabricated information). In synthetic
chemistry applications, FPs are typically considered more detrimental than FNs. Our prompting strategy
effectively guided the model to extract a variety of experimental data, including compound identifiers, quantities,
yields, solvents, reaction conditions, and enantiomeric excess (e.e.) values, achieving high precision, recall, and
F1 scores for nearly all categories(see more details in Supplementary Note 4.1 Table 2) The only discrepancy
was the misidentification of an uncommon solvent mixture or additive (e.g., 18-crown-6), indicating that the
model's performance critically relies on its pre-existing chemical knowledge. This limitation can be easily
addressed by enhancing the prompt with information about such uncommon entities.

The text mining pipeline was subsequently expanded to extract complex spectroscopic data (NMR, MS,
HPLC) by leveraging tailored prompts with GPT-4. We targeted characterization data for 236 molecules from
the SI of the same benchmark literature used previously and developed prompts for data mining, including 1H
NMR, MS, HPLC, and IR (see more details in SI 3.1-3.2). The system demonstrated high efficacy, with
extraction accuracies exceeding 95% for most spectroscopic types (Fig. 3a). Notably, despite the inherent
complexity of 1H NMR data, which requires parsing chemical shifts, splitting patterns, and coupling constants,
the accuracy of its extraction remained remarkably high. This success suggests that the structured prompts
enabled the LLM to effectively extract the in-context chemical knowledge inherent in spectroscopic reports (Fig.
3c). Error analysis highlighted challenges in classifying coupling constants (J-values) and resolving ambiguities
due to inconsistent compound labels. Subsequent analysis indicated that more advanced LLM architectures
exhibit greater robustness against such inconsistencies.

Standardization of Extracted Chemical Information: The conversion of diverse compound nomenclature
(including IUPAC names, common names, misspelled variants, and chemical formulas) into machine-readable
SMILES representations remains a significant challenge in organic reaction mining29. A critical component of
ReactionSeek is its data standardization module, which is designed to convert raw extracted text into an accurate,
consistent, and AI-ready format (Fig. 2c). The module emphasizes two primary curation tasks: name-to-SMILES
transformation and unit standardization.

General-purpose LLMs are often unreliable for direct name-to-SMILES transformation, a limitation rooted
in their generative instability and lack of domain-specific knowledge training. As reported in previous work39 ,
this deficiency results in a high frequency of critical errors, including unparsable strings, the addition or omission
of atoms, incorrect functional group placement, and erroneous backbone structures. Given these significant
reliability issues, the direct application of general-purpose LLMs for this conversion task is challenging.
ReactionSeek overcomes this by implementing a hybrid workflow: (1) First, unique compound names are
compiled from the mining results. (2) Second, these names are processed using established cheminformatics
resources, including database lookups (e.g., PubChem40) and name-to-structure converters (e.g., OPSIN41), to
generate canonical SMILES. (3) Finally, the LLM, enhanced with vector and fuzzy search capabilities,
intelligently maps the mined nomenclature, which is often non-standardized, to the canonical SMILES curated
by these specialized tools. This iterative process of data validation, parsing, and LLM-assisted alignment ensures
the generation of high-fidelity structural representations (Fig. 2c).

Simultaneously, the module leverages the LLM in unit standardization (Fig. 2c). Through carefully
designed prompts, it standardizes units for all reaction parameters (e.g., time, temperature) to ensure dataset-
wide consistency. The final output is a structured CSV file that summarizes each reaction using standardized
identifiers and parameters. This curated dataset is not only directly suitable for building predictive models but
also serves as the knowledge base for interactive tools such as the SynChat application.

Large-Scale Reaction Mining: A Case Study of the Organic Syntheses Collection30
To demonstrate the scalability and practical utility of ReactionSeek, we applied it to the systematic mining
of the Organic Syntheses collection30, a historically significant and high-quality repository of verified synthetic
procedures published since 1921. This collection, comprising 102 volumes as of 2025, represents a valuable
resource for studying the evolution of synthetic methodology. For this study, we processed 3,103 articles from
the first 100 volumes, establishing a comprehensive raw dataset for subsequent analysis and chatbot development
(see more details in Supplementary Figure 4). A benchmark subset of 50 articles from this collection was also
curated manually for detailed performance evaluation.

Efficiency of Automated Mining: A key advantage of ReactionSeek is its potential to significantly reduce
the time and effort associated with manual data extraction. On the 50-article benchmark set, using GLM-442, the
framework required an average of 21.32 seconds per article for data mining and output formatting. This
represents a substantial improvement over manual data mining, which typically requires 5-10 minutes or longer
per article, underscoring the efficiency gains enabled by our LLM-based approach.

Accuracy Assessment on Organic Syntheses30 Benchmark: We evaluated the accuracy of ReactionSeek
(with GLM-4) on the 50-article benchmark dataset, employing evaluation criteria tailored to the practical needs
of subsequent applications. (1) Reactants and Products: Correct and complete extraction and classification of all
compound entities involved as reactants or products were considered critical. (2) Reaction Yield: Precise
extraction of yield values. (3) Reaction Scale (Amounts): The focus was on accurately extracting amounts for
key reactants and products, with relaxed stringency for ancillary reagents, such as solvents or excess reagents,
where order-of-magnitude and proportional relationships are often sufficient. (4) Time and Temperature: Given
the potential variability in experimental records for these parameters, the model was assessed on its ability to
extract the critical time and temperature values it deemed necessary, rather than achieving absolute accuracy for
every recorded value.

As shown in Fig. 4a, GLM-4 demonstrated strong performance in compound identification, particularly for
products, with very few FPs in reactant extraction, meeting a key accuracy demand. However, some omissions
(FNs) occurred during reactant extraction, likely due to inconsistent textual positioning of reactants. The
occurrence of FPs in solvent identification suggested the LLM might rely on its a priori knowledge of common
solvents, potentially misclassifying uncommon solvents or reactants.

In numerical data extraction, the model showed high accuracy for reaction yields and product quantities,
with no instances of hallucinated yield values on the test set. A notable error pattern emerged in reactant quantity
extraction when a compound was added in multiple portions; the model often struggled to accurately aggregate
these amounts. This may reflect limitations in the LLM's complex numerical reasoning within linguistic contexts
or the absence of specific prompt engineering for such scenarios. Time and temperature extraction, although
facing similar complexities, benefited from being listed as separate extraction targets, resulting in comparatively
better performance.

Out of the 50 benchmark articles, 48 yielded outputs conforming to the required format after reprocessing
of any initially unparseable results. The two articles that failed to produce correctly formatted outputs were
significantly longer (9824 and 5502 characters, which may almost exceed the context window of the LLM) and
contained more reactions (5 reactions each) than average. In these cases, GLM-4 successfully extracted the
information but failed in formatting, suggesting that very long input texts following an already lengthy prompt
can lead to the model partially forgetting initial formatting instructions.43 Text segmentation is a potential
strategy to mitigate this issue.

Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Text Mining : The performance of LLM-based data mining is
significantly influenced by the choice of the underlying model, particularly its parameter size and architecture.
To guide model selection for ReactionSeek, we evaluated a diverse range of LLMs on the Organic Syntheses30
benchmark dataset. The models tested included GLM-4, GPT-3.544, GPT-445, Llama46, Mixtral47, Baichuan48,
Qwen49, and DeepSeek50.

Larger models generally exhibited significantly higher performance in extracting chemical information (Fig.
4a, 4d). This suggests that increased parameter size critically impacts an LLM's ability to understand complex
chemical contents. Larger models were better at understanding task objectives and correctly identifying relevant
chemical entities. Furthermore, the incidence of unparseable or incorrectly formatted responses decreased with
increasing model size (Fig. 4b). This improvement is likely due to the enhanced capacity of larger models to
handle long token inputs while retaining memory of key prompt instructions, and their superior ability to
comprehend complex chemical relationships and knowledge inherent in the context.

Interestingly, while larger models excelled in precision, medium-sized models often achieved comparable
recall rates (Fig. 4c). This indicates that once a model possesses a sufficient parameter scale to grasp the
fundamental chemical tasks outlined in the prompts, further size increases may offer diminishing profit for
simple identification tasks. Persistent error types, such as the aggregation of reactant quantities from multiple
additions, were not fully resolved solely by increasing model parameter size, highlighting the need for targeted
prompt refinements or algorithmic solutions for such specific challenges (Fig. 4b-d).

Analysis of successful extractions by small and medium-sized models revealed they typically performed
well in articles describing simpler reactions (e.g., fewer compounds, straightforward single-step procedures) and
those with shorter text lengths. This suggests that text segment length is a key factor influencing an LLM's ability
to generate valid, well-formatted outputs, as shorter texts reduce the cognitive and memory burden on the model.
For less complex extraction tasks or when using smaller models, strategies such as text segmentation or
employing models specifically adapted for long contexts can improve performance.

Based on the aforementioned evaluations, we ultimately employed GPT-3.5-16k to conduct data mining on
Organic Syntheses30 volumes 1–100, spanning from 1921 to 2021. After complete pipeline processing and
deduplication, we obtained 5,443 unique compounds, 3,961 unique reactions, of which 3,580 contained yield
information.

To demonstrate our pipeline's generalizability to newly published literature, we tested it on all newly
published articles (29 articles) from the 2025 volume of Organic Syntheses30 (Fig. 4e and Table 1). Our pipeline
correctly extracting most of reaction information from each article. During the standardization phase, with the
exception of molecular sieves that cannot be directly represented as SMILES, all other compounds were
successfully converted into their correct corresponding SMILES representations. These results confirm our
pipeline’s robustness, showing its ability to generalize effectively from benchmark datasets to newly published
chemical literature.

While modest in size compared to larger reaction databases like USSPTO, the value of our minded dataset
lies not in its breadth, but in its curated depth. It is composed of the most representative and classical organic
reactions across one century, with the exclusive inclusion of gram-scale procedures guaranteeing experimental
robustness and reproducibility. Consequently, we propose that this collection can serve as a standardized
reference for synthetic chemists and as a high-fidelity benchmark for the development and validation of machine
learning models.

LLM-Driven Discovery of Chemical Trends from Mined Data
To demonstrate the potential for data-driven discovery, we utilized ReactionSeek to create a large-scale,
structured dataset from the Organic Syntheses30 collection. This AI-ready dataset then served as the input for
autonomous analysis via Gemini 2.5 Pro.51 By designing specific prompts, we tasked the LLM with uncovering
historical trends within this century-spanning compendium, including the emergence and diversification of
asymmetric catalysis and the changing landscape of metal utilization in synthesis (Fig. 5).

In its analysis of asymmetric catalysis (Fig. 5b), the LLM identified a significant increase in such reactions
after 1980. It highlighted the pivotal role of transition-metal catalysts, alongside the emergence of organic small-
molecule catalysts and enzymatic/biocatalytic systems. The LLM noted the prevalent use of specific metals like
Boron, Copper, Titanium, Ruthenium, and Palladium, correlating their use with advancements in well-known
methodologies such as CBS reductions, metal-coupling protocols, asymmetric epoxidation (e.g., with Titanium
Tartrate or Ti-BINOL systems), asymmetric hydrogenation, cross-coupling reactions, and allylic alkylation.
Furthermore, the LLM identified substrate preferences, observing that aldehydes and ketones, as well as halides,
were the most dominant, with esters and alkenes also featuring prominently (see Supplementary Note 2.4 for
more details).

Regarding metal usage trends (Fig. 5b, 5d), the LLM's analysis revealed an interesting prevalence of tin in
specific periods, correctly attributing this to the widespread adoption of tributyltin hydride (Bu3SnH) as a mild
radical initiator, reducing agent, and key component in Stille couplings. More broadly, the LLM categorized the
evolution of metal usage in Organic Syntheses30 into three distinct epochs: (1) The Main-Group Metal Era (1921–
1960): Dominated by Grignard reagents and salt-forming reactions, with less emphasis on metal toxicity. (2) The
Incipient Transition (1961–1990): Characterized by the rise of lithium/copper reagents, the early development
of palladium catalysis, and a decline in mercury utilization. (3) The Golden Age of Transition-Metal Catalysis
(1991–2023): Marked by concentrated growth in Palladium-, Ruthenium-, and Rhodium-mediated
transformations.

These LLM-identified trends accurately reflect established paradigm shifts in organic synthesis from
stoichiometric to catalytic approaches, from harsh to milder conditions, and from highly toxic reagents towards
greener methodologies. This demonstrates that an LLM, when provided with a structured dataset curated by
ReactionSeek, can autonomously develop analytical insights and perform trend analyses consistent with expert
chemical knowledge, highlighting the potential for AI-assisted discovery from systematically mined literature.

The Synthesis Chatbot: Interactive Access to Mined Knowledge
To enhance the accessibility and utility of the extensive dataset curated from Organic Syntheses30, we
developed SynChat, an interactive tool powered by LLM agents. SynChat allows researchers to query the
historical reaction data and associated metadata using natural language, providing a more intuitive and efficient
means of accessing specific data compared to traditional search methodology.

The development of the chatbot involved structuring the mined data for effective retrieval by the LLM. Key
information from each reaction entry (e.g., title, DOI, reactants, products, SMILES, yield) was compiled and
vectorized to a customized vector database52.This allows the LLM, when presented with a user query, to perform
similarity searches across the Vector Database and retrieve the most relevant supporting texts from the original
Organic Syntheses30 (Fig. 6). The LLM agent then synthesizes an answer based on this retrieved information,
previous record and reasoning, with prompts designed to ensure strict adherence to the source material, thereby
minimizing the likelihood of generating hallucinated or inaccurate responses.

SynChat offers several advantages for chemical researchers: (1) Natural Language Queries with Molecular
Structures: It handles complex queries posed in natural language that incorporate molecular structures or reaction
information, increasing the flexibility of data access for users without specialized database query language skills.
(2) Enhanced Reliability and Traceability: By citing specific data sources from the Organic Syntheses30
collection, the chatbot allows users to consult the original literature for verification and further context easily.
(3) Iterative Information Retrieval: The interactive nature of the LLM enables users to refine their queries or ask
follow-up questions in multi-turn dialogues, facilitating a more thorough exploration of the available information.
This interactive tool exemplifies how LLMs can transform structured and unstructured data into dynamic
knowledge resources, bringing AI-powered assistance directly into the research and learning workflows of
organic chemists.

## Methods

Prompt Design for Image Mining
Image mining was conducted using the GLM-4V multi-modal large language model. To improve the logical
accuracy of the model in determining compound roles, we designed specific instructions requiring the LLM to
explicitly analyze the visual orientation of reaction arrows (e.g., distinguishing between reactants and products
based on arrow direction). Adopting the structured prompt framework utilized in our text mining workflow, the
image mining prompts were specifically tailored to extract the numerical labels associated with reactants,
products, and reagents from the reaction schemes. Following role identification, chemical structure recognition
was performed using InDraw,34 which automatically segmented and identified each compound structure before
converting them into canonical SMILES strings for storage. Full details regarding the prompt engineering
strategies and templates are provided in Supplementary Note 1.1.

Prompt Design for Text Mining
To extract detailed experimental procedures and reaction parameters from unstructured organic chemistry
literature with high fidelity, we developed a structured prompt engineering pipeline tailored for Large Language
Models (LLMs). This pipeline was designed to guide the LLM in identifying compound entities, resolving co-
reference relationships, and structuring extracted data into a standardized tabular format. The prompt architecture,
inspired by methodologies for metal-organic framework (MOF) data extraction17, consists of four strategic
components optimized for chemical text analysis:

1. Task Description: This module defines the global objective of the data mining task. It includes explicit
constraints and negative constraints to mitigate common LLM issues, such as hallucination, ensuring
the model focuses strictly on the provided text.
2. Task Requirements: To ensure output consistency, this module specifies the exact information fields to
be extracted and enforces a strict tabular output format. This instruction block is strategically positioned
within the prompt to reinforce the LLM’s adherence to formatting specifications, thereby counteracting
potential context forgetting (memory decay) associated with long input sequences.
3. Processing Suggestions: We incorporated expert-derived heuristics in natural language to aid the LLM.
These suggestions were developed through a pre-examination of representative literature by domain
experts, summarizing common textual patterns and embedding essential chemical knowledge to
facilitate the correct interpretation of complex chemical narratives.
4. Processing Cases (Few-Shot Learning): To facilitate in-context learning, we included a set of few-shot
examples consisting of raw input texts paired with their corresponding, manually verified structured
outputs. This module allows the LLM to learn specific input-output mappings and formatting
requirements by example.

To resolve complex co-reference relationships, the pipeline processes sub-headings and main text segments as
distinct but related inputs, enabling the model to associate compound references within the synthetic procedures
with their corresponding specific compounds defined in the sub-headings. Full details of the prompt templates
and specific examples are provided in Supplementary Note 1.2.

Data Standardization Design
The standardization process was carried out in three consecutive steps. In step (1), the chemical compound
dataset was created using compound names and their respective CAS numbers extracted from the Organic
Syntheses30 collection. Next, in step (2), compound identifiers were primarily obtained through CAS numbers,
followed by additional identification using PubChem40 nomenclature and OPSIN41 systematic name parsing for
unprocessed entries. In step (3), molecular name vectorization was conducted to produce a comprehensive
dataset, which allowed for precise matching of mined molecular names. For unit standardization, temporal values
were consistently converted into minutes, with particular attention given to unconventional temporal expressions,
such as "overnight". Similarly, material quantities were standardized by converting all measurements into
uniform units of grams and moles. Full details regarding the prompt engineering strategies and templates are
provided in Supplementary Note 1.1.

Design of SynChat
The reaction database is architected into two distinct components to optimize retrieval efficiency and
information density: a vectorized query database for semantic search and a supplementary metadata repository
for detailed experimental context.

(1) Vectorization and Indexing: Key retrieval fields—including product SMILES, ReactionSMILES,
chemical nomenclature, reaction types, and article titles—were vectorized using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model,
a Sentence-BERT (SBERT) framework. This model transforms input text into 384-dimensional dense vector
embeddings without dimensionality reduction. These embeddings were indexed and managed using
ChromaDB53, an open-source vector database, to facilitate high-speed semantic similarity search. The specific
distribution of these embedding vectors is visualized in Supplementary Note 5.

(2) Data Retrieval and Generation: Detailed experimental parameters, including full synthetic procedures,
yields, reagent quantities, reaction conditions, and citation metadata, are stored in the supplementary database in
a JSON file. Upon receiving a user query, the system executes a retrieval process that identifies relevant entries
based on vector similarity (semantic match) and exact character matching within the ChromaDB index. The
system then retrieves the corresponding comprehensive procedural details from the supplementary database.
Finally, the retrieved context—combining the concise query features and the full textual descriptions—is
concatenated and fed into the Large Language Model (LLM). This Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
approach enables the LLM to generate tailored, evidence-based responses to user inquiries regarding specific
reaction conditions and procedures.

helpful to report the proportion of successful versus failed extractions, and whether any fallback
strategies are in place.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer's careful reading of our repository and their pertinent
comments. Access to APIs such as OpenAI can be restricted or not stable in certain scenarios,
occasionally leading to request failures (Approximately 4.3% of requests failed in the first
round of our extraction process). The likelihood of such failures is significantly reduced,
however, with a stable network, etc. To handle these potential failures, we implemented an
exponential backoff strategy to manage transient network fluctuations. If a request still failed,
it was logged and the API call will be restarted. Using this two-tiered approach, we successfully
processed all content.

advantages in efficiency and adaptability. The key advantages, which are now detailed in the

1. On the ChEMU patent reaction mining benchmark, our framework achieves a state-of-the-
art F1 score of 0.983, outperforming the competition's top score of 0.968. Critically, this
was achieved via few-shot learning, requiring annotation of fewer than 10 examples. In
stark contrast, the benchmark models rely on extensive supervised training with large
datasets (e.g., ~900 labeled examples). This represents a dramatic reduction in data
annotation costs and effort, making our pipeline exceptionally transferable and practical,
especially in specialized domains where labeled data is scarce.
2. Our framework demonstrates superior versatility. By simply modifying the prompts and
providing a few relevant examples, the same underlying model can be adapted to diverse
text mining scenarios. As demonstrated in our work, this includes extracting information
from patent procedures, journal protocols, and even spectroscopic data in supporting
information. This adaptability stands in contrast to conventional models, which would
require re-training entirely new systems for each distinct task.
3. The combination of high data efficiency and versatility makes our approach particularly
powerful for specialized research areas particularly for synthetic methodology studies (e.g.,
mining reactions for a specific catalyst or reaction class, new reaction
development/optimization, synthetic route design). In these domains, the lack of large
annotated datasets often renders traditional data-hungry models ineffective. Our framework
provides a robust and scalable solution to this long-standing challenge.
We believe these additions and detailed explanations directly address the reviewer's concerns

Q3. Then, authors need to show which type of cases their approach can’t extract reactions and
whether they have taken care to improve those. For example, in the work
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-024-00928-8, fig 5, the authors identified
number of challenges for text to reaction extraction. Whether the proposed approach can
overcome them?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for their valuable suggestions regarding the challenges for
reaction extraction. Specifically, our work focuses on addressing: (1) the dispersion of
compound information across sub-headings and complex compound co-referencing, (2) name-
to-SMILES conversion, and (3) compound identification in reference images. To our
understanding, these may cover the five challenges identified in the mentioned reference (now
cited as ref. 29). We list herein a detailed discussions:
(1) the dispersion of compound information across sub-headings and complex
compound co-referencing: We employed a segregated input approach where sub-headings and
synthetic text are processed separately, enabling the LLM to effectively learn this
representational pattern. The relevant main text content is as follows (On page 5 of the main
text):
"... With this pipeline, the LLM can effectively identify compound entities within text
segments and establish their complex co-reference relationships. By processing sub-headings
and text segments separately, our pipeline successfully achieves the association between
compound references in synthetic text segments and the corresponding compounds mentioned
in sub-headings. ...."
(2) Chemical name-to-SMILES conversion: We developed a dedicated processing
module for transforming chemical nomenclature into SMILES notation. The corresponding
discussion in the main text is presented below (On page 7 of the main text):
"... The conversion of diverse compound nomenclature (including IUPAC names, common
names, misspelled variants, and chemical formulas) into machine-readable SMILES
representations remains a significant challenge in organic reaction mining. A critical
component of ReactionSeek is its data standardization module, which is designed to convert
raw extracted text into an accurate, consistent, and AI-ready format (Fig. 2c). The module
emphasizes two primary curation tasks: name-to-SMILES transformation and unit
standardization. ...."
(3) Identification of compounds in reference images: We developed an integrated
module utilizing VLM-assisted OCSR tools for information association. The system operates
through a multi-stage process: (i) the VLM component identifies textual and ideographic
elements within structural images, determining both the compounds' functional roles in
reactions and their corresponding identifiers; (ii) the OCSR module converts these identified
structures into SMILES notation. This pipeline enables the transformation of reaction
schematics into chemically interpretable SMILES relationships. The corresponding discussion
in the main text is presented below (On page 4 of the main text):
"... While existing Optical Character Structure Recognition (OCSR) tools can convert
molecular structures into machine-readable formats (e.g., SMILES), associating these
structures with their correct roles (e.g., reactant, product) and textual identifiers within complex
figures remains challenging. ...."
That said, there still some remaining challenges that warrants further explorations, and
these include: (1) handling uncommon chemical names and structures, (2) interpreting complex
contextual relationships dispersed across the paper, and (3) a reliance on the performance of the
underlying OCSR tool and LLMs. Our ongoing work is dedicated to addressing these
limitations to achieve more comprehensive and robust reaction mining from the literature. In
the Discussion section, we address these challenges of our current pipeline (On page 14 of the
main text):
"... Current limitations include challenges in (1) handling uncommon chemical names and
structures, (2) interpreting complex contextual relationships dispersed across the paper, and (3)
a reliance on the performance of the underlying OCSR tool and LLMs. For (1), the structural
elucidation of newly synthesized compounds presents significant challenges when these
compounds are neither registered in existing databases nor properly systematized through
standard nomenclature rules. For (2), for complex compound relationships presented in tables,
ReactionSeek still faces challenges in achieving satisfactory mining success rates. For (3),
currently available OCSR tools still face significant challenges in R-group identification and
complex structure recognition. Concurrently, the developmental stage of LLMs imposes
limitations on both the performance of LLMs and existing cheminformatic tools. ...."

authoritative ChEMU33-36, which achieved a top F1 score of 0.968 on key chemist-centric
