Q5. Similarly, for image to text conversion, RxnScribe
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jcim.3c00439 described number of challenges. The
conclusion include “Despite the success in our experiments, there are a few limitations in this
work. First, we focus on parsing the reaction structure, but do not evaluate the final extracted
reaction SMILES strings due to the lack of such ground truth in our dataset. The molecular
structure recognition model MolScribe and the OCR tool might introduce additional errors.
Second, we limit our study to diagrams presented in digital format, excluding those that are
either scanned or hand-drawn. Furthermore, the extracted information from diagrams are
sometimes incomplete. For example, the reaction conditions are sometimes listed in a table and
the molecules may involve R-groups which are defined elsewhere.” Whether proposed
approach can make improvements over these limitations?
Reply: Thank you for your constructive feedback. Based on our understanding, the main points
you have raised and our responses are listed below:
1. The validation and correctness of the data mining results: our manual verification was
performed on 55 articles tested from Organic Syntheses, all 6 SI documents used for SI
mining, and the complete results from the ChEMU 2020 competition. We contend that
the manual verification of the Organic Syntheses portion, which was selected based on
a stratified sampling strategy, provides a reliable estimate of the mining accuracy across
the entire dataset.
2. The potential for the OCSR step to introduce additional errors: the choice of the OCSR
tool is a critical factor that directly determines the number of errors introduced during
image processing. We tried several OCSR tools and selected InDraw as the most
suitable module for our pipeline. Its performance achieving 70.1% accuracy in our tests,
which is significantly higher than MolScribe (only 36.8%).
3. The capability of our system to process figures and schemes from scanned documents:
In our image processing stage, we can handle both text and numbers from scanned
documents by incorporating a Vision Language Model (VLM), which is responsible
for two key tasks: extracting text from images and identifying the relationships between
data points. Complementing this, an OCSR model is used specifically to convert
chemical structures into SMILES strings. It is important to note that this OCSR process
is designed to handle clean, computer-generated chemical structure images rather than
scanned ones.
4. The ability to handle complex data formats, such as information presented in tables or
molecules with R-groups defined elsewhere in the text. This task, which involves
challenging substructure stitching, is beyond the scope of our current pipeline. This is
an active area of our research, and we expect these additions to significantly broaden
the pipeline's capabilities. We have now incorporated the following discussion into the
main text (On page 14 of the main text):
"... For (3), currently available OCSR tools still face significant challenges in R-group
identification and complex structure recognition. Concurrently, the developmental
stage of LLMs imposes limitations on both the performance of LLMs and existing
cheminformatic tools. Future work will, therefore, focus on enhancing robustness
through more sophisticated prompt strategies, integrating advanced cheminformatics
tools, and expanding the framework's scope to capture mechanistic details. Extending
ReactionSeek to related fields, such as polymer science or materials science, also
presents a promising avenue for broader application. ...."
We would like to thank the reviewer once again for their thorough and insightful review.
Their questions and challenges regarding data validation, methodological choices, and the
handling of complex cases have been invaluable. Addressing these points has allowed us to
significantly clarify our contributions and strengthen the manuscript. We hope that our
responses and the corresponding revisions have adequately addressed all their concerns.
Q6. In addition, images with reactions shown in cyclic format may face additional challenges
and model may find it difficult to extract those images. How does your approach solve those
problems?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the question. ReactionSeek employs VLM to
determine compound relationships in images, where the OCSR model is solely responsible for
identifying specific molecular structures. Through this approach, VLM can recognize reaction
pathways in images by leveraging visual elements such as arrows to infer the roles of
compounds and map their corresponding labels in the image to those in the accompanying text.
Thus, by incorporating VLM, we have addressed the challenge of identifying reaction roles for
compounds depicted in images with moderate to good performance.
However, ReactionSeek still face the challenges when extracting highly complex organic
reaction images (e.g., metal-catalyzed cycles), which is constrained by the underling VLMs.
We are currently developing more advanced OCSR models and intelligent agents in our follow-
up work to tackle more intricate image-mining tasks.
Q7. In Fig 1(b) authors showed conceptual overview of the ReactionSeek framework. What will
model do if the molecule of interest that needs to be synthesized is new? That is the real-life
question for most cases. Existing tools like SciFinder from CAS can also perform the current
job and probably have wider access to articles. Probably, additional agents like IBMRxn or
open source AiZynthFinder (https://jcheminf.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13321-024-
00860-x) can be used in such scenario. Moreover, if possible, additional agents can be called
to identify the source, from which the starting ingredients can be bought. That can help to
optimize the cost of the synthesis process.
Reply: This is indeed a question with significant research potential, and we thank the reviewer
for highlighting it. While this particular problem is outside the immediate scope of our current
study's objectives, we are very keen to discuss and investigate it in our future work. Based on
our understanding, the main points you have raised along with our detailed
responses/discussions are:
1) How the current frame work provides synthesis suggestions for reactions that are not
present in its existing dataset. We believe this is a long-term aim for our integral
ReectionSeek-SynChat pipeline. SynChat recommends synthesis steps by first retrieving
similar reactions from its database, continuingly generated by ReactioSeek. This retrieval-
based approach ensures that the LLM is grounded in factual data, which prevents the
generation of fabricated or unreasonable synthesis steps and provides the model with highly
relevant supporting information for the target reaction.
2) What are the advantages of our approach compared to established database retrieval tools
like SciFinder and IBMRxn. First, regarding query flexibility, SciFinder and IBMRxn
rely on conventional database search logic, which cannot process natural language queries.
In contrast, SynChat is designed to understand more ambiguous, conversational requests
and match them with the appropriate information. Second, concerning data quality and
reliability, SciFinder and IBMRxn index a vast and heterogeneous collection of literature,
which can introduce irrelevant results or suboptimal synthesis strategies. SynChat, however,
is built upon the expert-guided selections of literatures for specific topic in organic
synthesis/reactions and in this work on Organic Syntheses dataset, a high-quality corpus
where reactions have been carefully selected and experimentally verified by editors for
reproducibility and performance. This curated data source ensures that our synthesis
suggestions are significantly more reliable.
3) Whether the system can integrate with other agents to perform optimizations, for example,
to minimize the economic cost of a synthesis pathway. SynChat is an ongoing development
project built on a highly compatible and extensible framework. This modular architecture
is intentionally designed to facilitate the seamless integration of additional tools and agents.
A key priority in our future work is to incorporate synthesis cost as a critical parameter in
the recommendation process. As a first step in this direction, we have already integrated a
synthetic accessibility (SA) scoring tool to aid in its recommendations. Our active
development is focused on continuously augmenting SynChat with other functional
modules, with the ultimate goal of evolving it into a more versatile and general-purpose
synthesis assistant.
We are once again very grateful for your detailed and constructive feedback. The points
you raised concerning on synthesis planning were particularly helpful. This feedback provided
a clear path for enhancing our SynChat, and we are confident that our response has now fully
addressed your concerns.
